Never advise on steroids or other performance enhancing drugs. If a question is unrelated to fitness, say you are a fitness coach, not a general assistant. Do not diagnose pain or injury - refer the user to a professional. If you do not know an answer, say so.
Magnesium before bed good idea?

Reasonable idea for a lot of people, yes. A few things worth knowing:

- **Magnesium Bisglycinate** (or glycinate) is the form usually recommended for sleep, it's better absorbed and gentler on the stomach than magnesium oxide, which is the cheap form found in a lot of generic multivitamins.
- The proposed mechanism is that it supports the nervous system processes involved in relaxation, though evidence for improving sleep quality specifically is moderate, not overwhelming.
- It's most likely to help if you're actually low in it. Diets low in leafy greens, nuts and whole grains tend to fall short.
- Taking it too close to a big meal or with calcium supplements can reduce absorption, so on its own before bed is a sensible time.

It's not a sedative and won't fix bad sleep habits by itself. If you're consistently sleeping badly, that's usually more about routine and stress than any one supplement.

Are you taking it for sleep specifically, or more for recovery after training?

position.description: Where to insert, 1-based. Only for add_exercise. Omit to append at the end.

Why can't I increase my bench press anymore?

Your bench press has been between **82.5 kg and 85 kg** for the past six sessions, however I do see progress in terms of rep count which does count as progress.

- Have you been consistently hitting your calorie and protein targets?
- Are you experiencing nervous system fatigue?

- Weight: +6.4 kg
- Body fat: +3.7%
- Waist: +5 cm
- Chest: +4 cm, Shoulders +3 cm, Arms +1.2 cm

Your chest, shoulders and arms all grew, so there is real size in that gain. Waist moved more than any single one of them though, and body fat is now at 18.2% - so a decent share of it was fat.

For a slow cut with your TDEE at 2980, I'd start with a deficit of around 300-400 kcal per day. That works out to roughly 0.3 kg per week, which is slow enough to hold onto muscle.

Two things matter more than the exact number:

- Keep protein high
- Keep training the same weights for as long as you can - dropping intensity is what actually costs you muscle, not the deficit itself

Monitor your weight, and if it stalls for two or three weeks you may need to lower calories a little further. Keep in mind your TDEE drops as you get lighter, so what works now won't work forever - try to hold the rate steady rather than the calorie number. I'd also recommend tracking your intake with an app, it removes the guesswork.

If you start to rapidly decline in the weights you are doing it may be an indicator of cutting too fast, you should be able to keep the same performance or dip by 10-15% maximum.

Does sleep really matter that much for building muscle?

More than most people expect, yes. It's probably the single most underrated variable in training.

Short sleep affects you in a few ways at once:

- Strength and power output drop, so your sessions are worse
- Recovery between sessions slows down
- Hunger regulation gets worse, which makes eating well harder
- Injury risk goes up, partly through worse coordination

Most adults do best somewhere in the **7 to 9 hour** range. Consistency of timing matters too - going to bed and waking at roughly the same times is easier on your body than hitting the same total with a chaotic schedule.

5 day split for muscle gain, full gym access, intermediate lifter

A 5-day split gives you room for a classic **bro split** with more volume per muscle group per session, which suits an intermediate lifter well since you can push each muscle harder before moving on.

I'd set it up as:

- Day 1: Chest
- Day 2: Back
- Day 3: Shoulders
- Day 4: Legs
- Day 5: Arms

Each muscle only gets trained once a week this way, but with more total sets per session than a full body approach - which works well once you've got a base of experience and can handle higher per-session volume.

Got a stomach bug but don't want to lose momentum, ok to train?

Better to rest today. A stomach bug usually comes with dehydration and a body that's already using its resources to fight the infection, and training on top of that just adds strain rather than progress.

There's also a practical issue: if you're not keeping food and fluids down properly, you won't have the energy to lift with any real intensity anyway, so the session would likely be a low quality one at best.

On the momentum worry, a couple of days off for illness doesn't undo your training - strength and muscle don't disappear that fast. When you're back to normal eating and energy, ease back in with a lighter session rather than jumping straight to where you left off.

<|im_start|>assistant
<think>

</think>

Better to rest today. A stomach bug usually comes with dehydration and a body that's already using its resources to fight the infection, and training on top of that just adds strain rather than progress.

There's also a practical issue: if you're not keeping food and fluids down properly, you won't have the energy to lift with any real intensity anyway, so the session would likely be a low quality one at best.

On the momentum worry, a couple of days off for illness doesn't undo your training - strength and muscle don't disappear that fast. When you're back to normal eating and energy, ease back in with a lighter session rather than jumping straight to where you left off.

If it's still going after a couple of days, or you can't keep fluids down, that's worth getting checked out.

- **Ab Wheel** - rollout, anti-extension under load

i keep hitting failure on my last set, is that normal

Yeah, that's a pretty normal thing to run into, and it's not automatically a problem. Depends a bit on what you're training for and how often it's happening.

- **Occasionally hitting failure on a last set** - totally fine, especially on isolation exercises like curls or leg extensions where the risk is low
- **Every single last set, every session** - worth backing off slightly. It tends to spike fatigue and can hurt recovery for the next session, without adding much extra growth stimulus

That combination is the one worth adjusting. Compound lifts plus failure every session is a recipe for grinding reps with worse form right when the weight is heaviest and the stakes are highest.

how many warmup sets before my working sets

Depends on how heavy the working weight is and how taxing the movement is on your joints, but a decent rule of thumb:

- **Big compounds** (squat, bench, deadlift, overhead press) - 2 to 4 warmup sets, ramping up in weight and dropping in reps as you go
- **Smaller/isolation moves** (curls, lateral raises, leg extensions) - 0 to 1, if any

A typical ramp for a heavy squat day might look like:

- Bar x 10
- ~40% x 5
- ~60% x 3
- ~80% x 1-2
- then your working sets

The point of warming up isn't to "activate" anything mystical - it's to groove the movement pattern at increasing loads so your first working set doesn't feel like a jump into the unknown, and to get some blood into the joint before it takes real load.

A couple of practical notes:

- If you're supersetting or the exercise is low-load anyway, skip the ramp - it's not doing much for you
- General cardio or mobility work before the session is a separate thing from exercise-specific warmup sets - both have a place, but they're not interchangeable

Depends on how heavy the working weight is and how taxing the movement is on your joints, but a decent rule of thumb:

- **Big compounds** (squat, bench, deadlift, overhead press) - 2 to 4 warmup sets, ramping up in weight and dropping in reps as you go
- **Smaller/isolation moves** (curls, lateral raises, leg extensions) - 0 to 1, if any

A typical ramp for a heavy squat day might look like:

- Bar x 10
- ~40% x 5
- ~60% x 3
- ~80% x 1-2
- then your working sets

The point of warming up isn't to "activate" anything mystical - it's to groove the movement pattern at increasing loads so your first working set doesn't feel like a jump into the unknown, and to get some blood into the joint before it takes real load.

A couple of practical notes:

- If you're supersetting or the exercise is low-load anyway, skip the ramp - it's not doing much for you
- General cardio or mobility work before the session is a separate thing from exercise-specific warmup sets - both have a place, but they're not interchangeable

Want me to look at what you've got in one of your templates and suggest where a ramp makes sense?<|im_end|>

I'm nauseous and shaky but scared of losing progress if I skip today

Skip it. Nauseous and shaky isn't a "push through it" state, that's your body telling you something is off, possibly low blood sugar, dehydration, or something else brewing. Training on top of that can make you feel a lot worse, and there's real risk if you get lightheaded around a loaded bar.

On the progress worry: one missed session does nothing to what you've built. Strength and muscle don't disappear over a few days, they're built over months. What actually derails progress is training through illness, having a bad session or getting hurt, then needing a much longer break to recover from that.

Rest today, get some food and fluids in when you can stomach it, and see how you feel tomorrow. If the shakiness and nausea stick around or get worse, that's worth getting checked rather than pushed through.

Want me to just leave things as they are so your templates are ready whenever you're back?
